title: Kotlin Multiplatform
subtitle: Shared code across iOS and Android

blocks.text: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) lets you write an app's non-UI code once in Kotlin and compile it into each platform's own binary format, so Android and iOS run the same business logic without a runtime bridge. It is an open-source technology from JetBrains, officially supported by Google for sharing code between Android and iOS.

The core idea is different from Flutter or React Native: KMP shares logic by default and leaves the UI decision to you. You can keep SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose, share the UI with Compose Multiplatform, or mix both screen by screen.

items: **Best fit:** teams with Kotlin skills, an existing native app, or a product where native look, platform APIs and long-term maintainability matter more than raw time-to-first-release.
**Weakest fit:** a solo developer or small Dart/JS team that needs one UI on both stores as fast as possible.

**Typical sharing:** networking, persistence, models, validation, state and business rules. A common planning figure is 60 to 80% of the codebase with native UI, and more with shared UI; treat it as a rule of thumb, not a measurement.

blocks.text: Traditional mobile development means two apps: Kotlin with Jetpack Compose on Android, Swift with SwiftUI on iOS. Every rule exists twice, and the two copies drift.

blocks.text: KMP removes that duplication while avoiding three costs that older cross-platform tools carry:

items: **No bridge or bundled engine for logic.** Shared code compiles to JVM bytecode on Android and to a native binary on iOS.
**No rewrite.** You can start with one module inside an existing app and expand later.
**No UI lock-in and no plugin wait.** Platform APIs are callable directly from Kotlin, so a new iOS or Android API does not need a third-party wrapper first.

lessons.title: Architecture: what is shared and what stays native

blocks.text: A KMP app is a sandwich: a native UI on top, platform glue at the bottom, and one shared Kotlin module in the middle that holds everything the two apps would otherwise duplicate. KMP app architecture · 2 native UIs, 1 shared module, 2 platform source sets
Read it top down: each UI calls the same shared module, and the shared module reaches the operating system only through small `expect` / `actual` declarations implemented per platform.

blocks.text: A practical rule: if a piece of code would produce a bug report that says "works on Android, wrong on iOS", it belongs in `commonMain`.
KMP has no runtime of its own: the Kotlin compiler has several backends, and each one turns the same shared source into the format that platform already runs.
KMP build pipeline · 3 source sets, 2 compilers, 2 shipped binaries
`commonMain` is compiled twice, once with each platform's source set, so neither app carries a bridge, an interpreter or a second UI engine for its logic.

blocks.text: Three consequences worth knowing before you start:

items: **Memory:** Kotlin/Native has its own tracing garbage collector. It coexists with Swift's ARC, so object lifetimes across the boundary are managed for you, but very allocation-heavy loops behave differently than on the JVM.
**Build time:** the iOS framework build is the slow step. Keep the exported API small and build only the simulator architecture you need during development.
**Debugging:** you can set breakpoints in shared Kotlin from Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin while running the iOS app.

blocks.text: A KMP module is a set of folders called source sets; the compiler decides which targets each folder is compiled for, and code flows down the hierarchy from common to specific.

blocks.code:
my-app/
├── shared/                      # the KMP module
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   └── src/
│       ├── commonMain/kotlin/   # shared logic: compiled for every target
│       ├── commonTest/kotlin/   # shared tests: run on every target
│       ├── androidMain/kotlin/  # Android-only code and actuals
│       ├── iosMain/kotlin/      # code shared by all iOS targets
│       └── iosTest/kotlin/
├── androidApp/                  # Android app: Jetpack Compose UI
└── iosApp/                      # Xcode project: SwiftUI UI

blocks.text: A minimal `shared/build.gradle.kts`. Version numbers are left out on purpose: take the current ones from the project wizard or a version catalog.

items: **Default hierarchy:** declaring `iosArm64()` and `iosSimulatorArm64()` creates the intermediate `iosMain` set automatically, so you do not wire `dependsOn` by hand.

**Rule for** `commonMain` **:** only Kotlin standard library and multiplatform libraries are visible. `java.*`, `android.*` and `platform.UIKit.*` do not compile there, which is what keeps the code portable. **Getting into Xcode:** the usual options are direct integration (an Xcode build phase runs Gradle's `embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode` task), an XCFramework published as a Swift package, or CocoaPods for projects that already use it.
**Starting point:** generate the skeleton with the Kotlin Multiplatform wizard in Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA instead of writing the Gradle files by hand.

blocks.text: Shared code declares what it needs with `expect`; each platform source set supplies it with `actual`, and the compiler refuses to build until every target has one.
Declare the need once, in `commonMain`:
Implement it on Android with Android APIs:
Implement it on iOS by calling Apple frameworks directly from Kotlin:

blocks.code:
// iosMain
import platform.UIKit.UIDevice
actual fun platformName(): String =
    UIDevice.currentDevice.systemName() + " " +
UIDevice.currentDevice.systemVersion

blocks.text: That last snippet is the "direct platform access" claim made concrete: `platform.UIKit`, `platform.Foundation`, `platform.CoreBluetooth` and the rest are available in `iosMain` without a plugin. **Prefer an interface when you can.** For most cases an ordinary interface in `commonMain` plus dependency injection is easier to test and to fake than `expect class`:

The Android implementation lives in `androidMain`; the iOS one can be written in Kotlin in `iosMain`, or in Swift in the iOS app and passed in at startup. Writing it in Swift is the right call when the SDK you wrap is Swift-only.

lessons.title: iOS interop: how Swift sees your Kotlin

blocks.text: The quality of the Swift-facing API decides whether iOS developers accept KMP, and there are three ways to produce it today.

rows: An Objective-C header that Swift imports
Exhaustive Swift enums for sealed classes, `async` for `suspend`, `AsyncSequence` for `Flow`
You ship today and want idiomatic Swift
Real Swift modules with no Objective-C header; `suspend` as `async`, `Flow` as `AsyncSequence`
You are evaluating, or on a new module you can afford to rework

blocks.text: What the Objective-C bridge loses, and why iOS developers on r/swift call the interop awkward:

items: **Generics** are only partly preserved, so collection and wrapper types reach Swift with less type information.
**Nullable primitives** such as `Int?` arrive boxed ( `KotlinInt?`) instead of as a Swift optional.
**Sealed classes and enums** do not become exhaustive Swift enums, so `switch` needs a `default`.
**Top-level functions** appear as members of a generated class named after the file ( `PlatformKt.platformName()`).
`suspend` **functions** surface as completion handlers; `Flow` has no built-in Swift equivalent.

blocks.text: Swift export limits to know before adopting it: it and Objective-C export are mutually exclusive in a module, exported classes are `final` on the Swift side (no cross-language inheritance yet), and JetBrains' Alpha label means the design can still change. The JetBrains roadmap published in August 2025 aimed for a stable release during 2026; as of this guide it is Alpha.
Five habits that make any route pleasant for the iOS team:
1. Keep the exported surface small: export a facade module, mark everything else

items: `internal`.

blocks.text: 2. Expose state as one `StateFlow<UiState>` per screen instead of many callbacks.
3. Prefer concrete types over generics at the boundary. 4. Use `@ObjCName` to give types and parameters Swift-friendly names, and `@Throws` on

items: functions whose exceptions Swift should catch.

blocks.text: 5. Add a thin Swift wrapper (an `ObservableObject` or `@Observable` class) around each

items: shared ViewModel, and let SwiftUI talk only to that.

blocks.text: How Compose Multiplatform relates to what you already know:

items: It is JetBrains' port of Jetpack Compose. The same `@Composable` APIs run on Android (as Jetpack Compose itself), iOS, desktop and web.
On iOS it renders through Skia, the same model Flutter uses with its own engine, so the "KMP means native widgets" claim holds only for the native-UI strategy.

iOS support has been Stable since Compose Multiplatform 1.8.0 (May 2025); the web target is in Beta. Interop works both ways: `UIKitView` embeds a native view (maps, camera preview, a WebView) inside Compose, and `ComposeUIViewController` embeds a Compose screen inside a SwiftUI or UIKit app.

blocks.text: A default that works for most teams: share everything up to and including ViewModels, start with native UI on iOS if you have iOS developers, and move individual low-risk screens to Compose Multiplatform once the shared layer is stable.
The ecosystem now covers every layer of a typical app; these are the mainstream choices, and klibs.io is the search index for everything else.

blocks.text: Before adding any dependency to `commonMain`, check that it publishes artifacts for every target you build. A JVM-only library there is the most common cause of a broken iOS build.

lessons.title: KMP vs Flutter vs React Native vs fully native

blocks.text: Yes, Flutter can build the same iOS and Android app from one codebase; the difference is what gets shared and who draws the pixels.

rows: Skia canvas on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android
Add to an existing native app

blocks.text: Two corrections to common talking points, so the comparison stays fair:

items: Flutter's Dart code is compiled ahead of time to native machine code, and current React Native uses a direct JavaScript interface instead of the old asynchronous bridge. "KMP is native, the others are bridged" overstates the gap for everyday screens.

App-size and startup differences are real but modest for most apps: Flutter and Compose Multiplatform on iOS both bundle a rendering engine; KMP with native UI adds only the Kotlin runtime and your shared code.

blocks.text: Where the gap is practical instead of theoretical: KMP wins on gradual adoption, direct platform APIs and keeping OS-native UI; Flutter wins on single-team velocity, a mature single-language toolchain and pixel-identical branded UI.

lessons.title: When to choose KMP, and when not to

blocks.text: Choose KMP when the cost you want to remove is duplicated logic; choose something else when the cost is building two UIs with a small team.

blocks.text: Three questions that settle most cases:
1. **Who will own the shared module?** KMP needs at least one engineer comfortable with

items: Kotlin and Gradle, and an iOS developer willing to shape the Swift-facing API.

blocks.text: 2. **How much of the app is logic?** A thin client over a REST API gains less than an app

items: with sync, pricing rules or offline state.

blocks.text: 3. **Does native UI matter to users?** If yes, KMP with native UI is the only cross-platform

items: option that keeps it by default.

blocks.text: Incremental adoption is KMP's strongest practical advantage: start with one module in the apps you already ship and stop at whichever phase stops paying off.
KMP adoption path · 4 phases, a gate after each Each phase is useful on its own, so a team that stops after phase 2 still has one data layer instead of two.

blocks.text: KMP's logic sharing has been Stable since late 2023 and is production technology; the parts still moving are Swift export and the web target.
